what: MIT's START natural-language system went online on the Internet in 1993 and answered English questions on many topics (Boris Katz, MIT)

sources.title: Boris Katz
sources.quote: Boris Katz is the creator of the START information processing system (since 1993 - on the Internet)

sources.title: Boris Katz
sources.quote: START natural language system that allows the user to access various types of information using English

note: START (1993) answered open-ended English questions about places, people, movies and more over the Web, an earlier broad-domain system than Watson 2011; its knowledge came from hand-annotated sources so breadth is limited (hence low). BASEBALL 1961, LUNAR 1971, SHRDLU, Unix Consultant and LILOG are narrow-domain; Ask Jeeves 1996 matched questions to web pages; Wolfram Alpha 2009 and Watson 2011 are later.

what: Sony Data Discman DD-1, a handheld electronic book player reading books on mini-CD, sold in Japan in 1990

sources.title: Sony Data Discman
sources.quote: The DD-1 was the earlier Japanese model in 1990.

sources.title: Sony Data Discman
sources.quote: is an electronic book player developed and marketed by Sony Corporation

note: Earlier than Rocket eBook 1998; Wikipedia's E-reader article lists the Data Discman among the first commercial e-readers. Later Western release 1991/92. Pre-1990 portable electronic book devices (e.g. Franklin dictionaries, Sony 1980s) not found in a fetched source.

what: Sony Librie in Japan, first e-book reader with an E Ink electronic paper display

sources.title: Electronic paper
sources.quote: In 2004, Sony released the Librié in Japan, the first e-book reader with an electronic paper E Ink display.

note: Checked Gyricon (Xerox PARC, 1970s lab prototype; Gyricon LLC signs sold in the 2000s, no fetched date earlier than 2004) and E Ink (founded 1997; first fetched commercial product Librie 2004, Motorola F3 2006). No fetched earlier practical product; Librie kept.

what: Lloyd Cross produced a hologram recreating a moving 3-dimensional image (Multiplex hologram, viewable around a cylinder)

sources.title: Holographic display
sources.quote: 1972 - Lloyd Cross produced the first traditional hologram by using white-light transmission holography to recreate a moving 3-dimensional image.

note: 1989 MIT electroholography is a lab system, not practical use. The 1972 Cross moving-image hologram is the earliest fetched 3D hologram display shown to the public (holography art exhibitions from 1968, per Wikipedia Holography, are static plates). Judgement call: practical use is thin, so low.

what: Manchester Baby (SSEM) had an output CRT displaying the bit pattern of its stores, from which results were read (working June 1948)

sources.title: Manchester Baby
sources.quote: was used as the output device, able to display the bit pattern of any selected storage tube

note: Whirlwind 1949 is a later display of a computed solution; the Baby's fourth CRT was dedicated output showing the machine's data to its operator, which fits 'screen shows data to its user' though only as bit patterns (hence low). EDSAC/Mark 1 CRTs are 1949 or later.

what: Whirlwind became operational in 1951, real-time output on CRT displays used in Cape Cod radar tracking

sources.title: Whirlwind I
sources.quote: Operational in 1951, it was among the first digital electronic computers that operated in real-time for output

note: Looked for earlier practical use of screens: Manchester Baby 1948 and Williams tubes were demonstration/engineering. SAGE and the Cape Cod system displays are same era or later. Date kept as an approximation.

what: E. A. Johnson (Royal Radar Establishment, Malvern) published a finger-driven capacitive touchscreen for air traffic control

sources.title: Touchscreen
sources.quote: He described his work on capacitive touchscreens in a short article published in 1965

note: Earlier: Philco 1946 stylus patent (overlay on TV, not touch input), AT&T Harmon 1962 light-beam patent (patent only, no working system shown), Graham 1963 light-pen patent. Johnson 1965 is the first finger-driven touchscreen per Wikipedia. Gesture side: nothing earlier controlling a machine fits (theremin is a musical instrument, not machine control).

what: PLATO IV terminals, introduced at the University of Illinois in 1972, had a built-in 16x16 infrared touch panel students used to answer questions

sources.title: PLATO (computer system)
sources.quote: In 1972, with the introduction of PLATO IV, Bitzer declared general success

sources.title: PLATO (computer system)
sources.quote: Touch panel: A 16×16 grid infrared touch panel, allowing students to answer questions by touching anywhere on the screen.

note: CERN's touchscreen was put to use in 1973; PLATO IV touch panels were part of the 1972 classroom system (Wikipedia Touchscreen dates the optical patent filing to 1972). Johnson's ATC touchscreen and the 1970 Telefunken device were described in the 1960s-70 but no fetched source gives deployed use earlier.

what: Touchscreen phones were rapidly gaining popularity by 2009 after the 2007 LG Prada and iPhone

sources.title: Touchscreen
sources.quote: By 2009, touchscreen-enabled phones were rapidly gaining popularity

note: Earlier touchscreens in ATMs, kiosks, HP-150 (1983), IBM Simon (1993), Nintendo DS (2004) were niche or early-stage, not routine use by ordinary people; 2009 majority of smartphones shipping with touchscreens (Wikipedia) supports 2007-2009 as the mass-adoption window.

what: Students at Evanston Township High School (Chicago suburb) penetrated IBM's APL network in fall 1967, the first known network penetration

sources.title: Timeline of computer security hacker history
sources.quote: The first known incidence of a kind of hacking called network penetration took place when members of a computer club

sources.title: Timeline of computer security hacker history
sources.quote: In the fall of 1967, IBM, (through Science Research Associates), approached Evanston Township High School

note: Morris worm 1988 is far later. Elk Cloner 1982, Brain 1986 and Creeper 1971 (experimental, harmless) are later; the 1965 CTSS password-file flaw was a bug found by staff, 1963 MIT phone/PDP-1 war dialing targeted phone lines. The 1967 Evanston intrusion into a live commercial computer service is the earliest fetched break-in; low because the source gives the date only loosely.

what: Bell Labs' Audrey, built by Balashek, Biddulph and Davis, recognized spoken digits from a single speaker.

sources.title: Speech recognition
sources.quote: 1952 – Bell Labs researchers, Stephen Balashek, R. Biddulph, and K. H. Davis, built Audrey for single-speaker digit recognition.

note: Radio Rex (1922) responds to acoustic energy, not words, so rejected; no earlier word-recognizing machine found in fetched sources. Wikidata quote not verifiable so dropped.

what: The Apricot Portable shipped with voice-command recognition (up to 4096 words, 64 in RAM at a time).

sources.title: Speech recognition
sources.quote: 1984 – the Apricot Portable was released with up to 4096 words support, of which only 64 could be held in RAM at a time.

note: Threshold Technology VIP-100 (about 1972) is credited by secondary sources as the first commercial speech recognition product, but its hosts are blocked here and no fetched page gives a quote or date, so it cannot be substituted. Apricot Portable 1984 kept as an upper bound; true first use probably earlier.
